ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Portal hypertension: 4

A patient with advanced portal hypertension has prominent radiating veins around the umbilicus. Which anatomical adaptation best explains this finding rather than interpreting it as a primary disease of the abdominal skin?

  1. Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration
  2. Portal-hypertensive ascites
  3. Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy
  4. Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals
  5. Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices
Answer and explanation

Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals

Dilated periumbilical veins can reflect collateral flow in portal hypertension.

Option explanations

Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals: Dilated periumbilical veins can reflect collateral flow in portal hypertension.

Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices: Elevated portal pressure can dilate collateral veins and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration: Portal hypertension can enlarge the spleen and contribute to thrombocytopenia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Portal-hypertensive ascites: Portal pressure and sodium-retaining responses contribute to ascites. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy: Blood bypassing hepatic clearance can contribute to encephalopathy, including after TIPS. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
